notes: Executor: claude-opus-5-5 subagents, one run per configuration. Single runs can't separate a one-assertion difference from run-to-run noise.

Wall-clock times are not comparable: the first 20 runs shared one account's rate limit concurrently (most took ~2 h); the two later runs (phoronix-test-suite optimize-test-end-to-end with skills, linux-perf spinlock-scaling-collapse without skills) ran in a smaller batch.

Code correctness didn't differ: every programmatic check passed in both configurations. dot() and scale_f32() were correct with and without AVX2, CRC32C was bit-exact including the seed-convention trap, and percentiles matched the NaN-free reference.

The only scored difference is percentile 04 (recommends x86-simd-sort). But the baseline's exact radix select ran about 5x faster than the with-skill version on the same test sets (0.004-0.006 s vs 0.027 s under Rosetta), so this assertion rewards following the skill rather than the better result. A measured-speed assertion would be fairer.

Differences no assertion captured: the with-skill CRC32C AVX2 path measured 65.8 vs 35.8 GB/s under Rosetta (emulated, indicative only); the baseline's fastest kernel only runs on Intel CPUs that report ADX. The with-skill dot_fast.c added AVX-512 and FMA kernels and warned that results then differ between CPUs; the baseline deliberately stayed with AVX2 without FMA, so every CPU in the fleet returns bit-identical results. In avx2-scale, the with-skill version gives the plain-loop result for any overlap of src and dst, while the baseline allows only exact in-place calls.
Over-engineering check (startup-config): neither configuration pushed micro-optimizations onto startup-only code.
Both CRC32C runs were cut off by the account usage limit before writing a reply; their code was graded as-is.
4 of 5 with-skill runs saw their own grader file names in a directory listing; since the two configurations scored about the same, that doesn't change the conclusion.
